claims.text: The protective coating is a dual-phase FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy.
A stable nanoscale oxide layer governs the coating's creep resistance under continuous loading.
Elevated temperature and a controlled environment promote formation of the nanoscale oxide layer.
The nanoscale oxide layer acts as a barrier to dislocation movement.
The nanoscale oxide layer acts as a barrier to grain-boundary sliding.
Reduced dislocation movement improves creep resistance.
Reduced grain-boundary sliding improves creep resistance.
Oxide-layer formation reduces progressive plastic deformation.
A coating with the oxide layer will exhibit greater creep resistance than the starting baseline without the oxide layer.
A coating with the oxide layer will exhibit less progressive plastic deformation than the starting baseline.
The proposed behavior is limited to temperature and stress ranges over which the oxide layer remains stable.
Alloy composition, microstructure, and loading conditions may affect oxide-layer formation and stability.
Samples with and without the oxide layer can be compared by nanoindentation and microcompression under sustained loading.
Removal or disruption of the oxide layer followed by a significant decrease in creep resistance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that the oxide layer increases creep resistance relative to an oxide-free baseline. Therefore, decreased creep resistance after removing or disrupting the oxide would support, not falsify, the hypothesis. Falsification would instead require no meaningful reduction, or an improvement, after oxide removal under an otherwise controlled comparison.
